attributes.title: Level 3

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Does the [forever] loop have two [show long text] code blocks with string values?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What type of message might you use to begin the Mad Libs story?

❓ Did you type the provided string values into the [show long text] blocks?

❓Does the text appear as you expected it would on the screen? Why or why not?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja to input the provided string values in the second [show long text] block exactly. If they input them incorrectly, prompt the ninja to notice which words should be spaced differently and/or where punctuation is needed.

💡The strings “NAME” and “ FEELING “will serve as placeholders for variables (of the same name) that will be added in later steps.

💡 Point out to the Ninja how the (join) block switches to a vertical orientation, when 5 or more bubbles are added.
steps.instructions:
Begin the Mad Libs project by writing a story! 


Drag a [show long text] block into the [forever] loop and update the location parameter. Edit the location parameter so that the dialog box appears in a helpful location on the screen. Type an introduction such as “Hello world! I have a story to tell you!” into the parameter. 


Drag another [show long text] block into the [forever] loop. Click Advanced at the bottom of the code block menu, open Text, then drag a (join) block into the parameter of the [show long text] block. Click + three times to make 5 total bubbles.


Type the following strings into 5 separate bubbles:

“One day, “ 

“NAME” 

“ was feeling ” 

“ FEELING ” 

“.” 


Click ▶ to see what appears in the dialog boxes on the screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you duplicate the [show long text] code block three times and type the string values of the Mad Libs story in each of the (join) blocks?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓Do the sentences of the Mad Libs story make sense right now? What do you think will replace the strings with all capital letters?

❓How will your story end? What type of sentence will you write that incorporates a “THING”? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Encourage the ninja to reread the sentences that appear in each of the dialog boxes, to ensure they appear correctly (except for the missing words). If they wish, the ninja can modify and personalize the sentences to make the Mad Libs story more interesting!
steps.instructions:
Continue writing the Mad Libs story!


Drag another [show long text] block with a (join) block inside into the [forever] loop. Update the location parameter, then duplicate the entire block two more times, inside the loop.


In the third [show long text] block, type the following strings into 3 separate bubbles: 

“So, they decided to go to the ” 

“PLACE”

“.”


In the fourth [show long text] block, type the following strings into 3 separate bubbles: 

“While there, they worked on the most amazing, most incredible, most fabulous ”

 “THING”

“ Code Ninjas had ever seen before!”  


In the fifth [show long text] block, use separate bubbles to type an ending to the story, making sure to include the word “THING” in its own white bubble.


Click ▶ to see what appears in the dialog boxes on the screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you move all of the [show long text] code blocks into the [if then] conditional?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What condition needs to be met in order for the story to appear on the screen?

❓ Why do you think it will be helpful to wait until there are no more teal button tile locations on the tilemap to show the story?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The [if then] conditional is constantly checking whether the number of teal button tiles on the tilemap is equal to zero. Later on, the project will turn the button tile into a path tile, once the user has provided a response.
steps.instructions:
Use a conditional so the story does not appear until the missing words have been filled in! 


Drag an [if then] conditional into the [forever] loop, then move all of the [show long text] blocks into it. 


Replace <true> with a <0=0> comparison block. Open Arrays and drag a (length of array) block into the left parameter of the <0=0> comparison block.


Open Scene and replace (list) with an (array of all tile locations) block. Delete (list) as needed, then click the tile dropdown menu and select the teal button tile.


Click ▶ to see the starting tilemap without any dialog boxes.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you create 2 text list arrays, one with the four strings: “name”, “feeling”, “place”, and “thing”, and one that is empty?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What is different about using the [set text list to] block instead of using the [set list to] block?

❓ Why do you think it will be helpful to begin the project with an empty array? How do you think it will be filled?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 By creating a text list, the ninja is telling the program that the array will contain string values, rather than numerical ones.

💡 Encourage the ninja to make a connection between the words (in all caps) included in the Mad Libs story and the strings entered into the text list. 

💡 Point out to the Ninja how the [set text list to] block switches to a vertical orientation, when 4 or more elements are added.
steps.instructions:
Create a text array to replace the missing words! 


Open Arrays and drag out a [set text list to] block into the [on start] container. Click + so there are 4 text bubbles.


Type the following strings into the 4 text bubbles in order: 

“name” 

“feeling” 

“place” 

“thing”


Drag another [set text list to] block into the [on start] container. Name the new text array “userResponseList.” Open Arrays and drag an (empty array) bubble into the [set userResponseList to] block.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you check the sequence of value blocks in the [list add value to end] block to make sure each is placed in the correct bubble?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓What appears on the screen, when the Player overlaps with the teal button tile?

❓What is added to the userResponseList, when the Player overlaps with the teal button tile?

❓Why do you think it will be important to both get and remove the first value from the text list, when the Player overlaps with the teal button tile?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Point out to the ninja how sequence matters in this context. The placement of each of the value blocks within the corresponding bubbles will impact what values are added to the userResponseList. Prompt the ninja to consider what would happen if they rearranged the (ask for string), (join), and (get and remove first value from list) blocks.
steps.instructions:
Ask for user input when the Player sprite overlaps each of the 4 teal button tiles! 


Open Arrays and drag the [list add value to end] block into the [on sprite overlaps tile] container. Click the drop-down on the variable list and select “userResponseList.” 


Open Game and drag an (ask for string) value block into the parameter in the [list add value to end] block. Drag a (join) block into the parameter of the (ask for string) value block. Write “Type a(n) “ in the first bubble. This will add the user's responses to the [userResponseList] text list, which will then be used in the completed story.


Open Arrays and drag the (get and remove first value from list) block into the second bubble of the (join) block. Select [text list] from the drop-down on the variable list. 


Click ▶ and move the Player sprite to overlap the teal button to provide user input!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add a [set tile at location] block, with the gray floor tile selected and the location value for the coordinate?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why does changing the tile at the overlap location fix this bug?

❓ What else might happen once the user has provided a response?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Guide the ninja in using the on screen keyboard to test out their project. They can use the direction buttons and A button to move the cursor on the screen and select the letters they’d like. They can select ABC to find capital letters and other characters to use in their response.
steps.instructions:
Oh no! The program is asking for all 4 missing words at once since the overlap continues to happen. Replace the tile image to stop the overlap. 


Open Scene and drag a [set tile at] block into the [on sprite overlaps tile] container. Drag the (location) bubble into the coordinate parameter. Select the gray floor tile. 


Click ▶ to see how the teal button tile turns into a gray floor tile after you provide user input for the missing words.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you leave the index used in the (get value at index) value block set to 0?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What shows up on the screen once you’ve added the (get value at index) value block into the [show long text] block?

❓ Does the sentence appear as you expected it would? Do you need to add any spacing or punctuation to make the sentence complete?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Since an array is an ordered list, each item has a number, or index, assigned to it, indicating its place in the list. The ninja is able to add, remove, retrieve, and reorder values in the list, based on its index.

💡 After the (get value at index) value block has been placed, encourage the ninja to test out the project to ensure it is formatted correctly. Prompt the ninja to add any needed spacing or punctuation to the strings in the [show long text] block.
steps.instructions:
Use each element’s array index to update the missing words in the story!


Notice there are 4 words in the story that need to be replaced, and there are 4 words in the text list array. Each element in an array is assigned an index. In computer science, an array index starts at 0 rather than 1. 



Open Arrays and drag a (get value at index) value block into the text bubble for “NAME” in the [show long text] block. Select “userResponseList” from the dropdown, and leave the value set to 0. This gets the first string saved in the array, “name.” 


Click ▶ to see how the element saved at array index 0 replaces “NAME” in the [show long text] block.

steps.hints: ❓ In each (get value at index) value block, did you set the correct list name and value?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What shows up on the screen once you’ve added the (get value at index) value block into the [show long text] blocks?

❓ Do the sentences appear as you expected they would? Do you need to add any spacing or punctuation to make the sentences complete?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Since an array is an ordered list, each item has a number, or index, assigned to it, indicating its place in the list. The ninja is able to add, remove, retrieve, and reorder values in the list, based on its index.

💡 After the (get value at index) value blocks have all been placed, encourage the ninja to test out the project to ensure they are formatted correctly. Prompt the ninja to add any needed spacing or punctuation to the strings in the [show long text] blocks.
steps.instructions:
Add the remaining user input into the story!


Replace the text “FEELING” with a (get value at index) value block that is set to the “userResponseList” and set it to 1. This gets the second string saved in the array, “feeling.”


Replace the text “PLACE” with a (get value at index) value block set to the “userResponseList” at value 2. This gets the third string saved in the array, “place.”


Replace both instances of “THING” with (get value at index) value blocks set to the value in the “userResponseList” for the last string saved in the array. 


Click ▶ to see how the user input is now part of the story!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add a [show long text] block to the [on start] container and a [game over] block to the [forever] loop?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What directions will help people understand how your project works?

❓ What else could you add to the Mad Libs story to make it more interesting?

❓What other effects might you add to enhance the project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Guide ninjas to note that while these customizing blocks are open-ended and not required for the game to “work”, they really improve the Player’s experience playing a game, either by giving context to what the Player should do or not do, or to provide a more fun experience overall. They also allow the Ninja to add their personal touch and express themselves through small details present in the game.
steps.instructions:
Code the beginning and end of the project!


Add a [show long text] to the beginning of the [on start] container block and write directions to guide game players. 


Drag [use effect] and [game over] blocks into the bottom of the [if then] conditional, and feel free to add more [show long text] blocks to customize this project.


Click ▶ to see the entire completed project!

subgroups.introduction: Build a project that asks users to fill in missing words and uses an array to create a complete story!

validationItems.text: Use dialog boxes to tell a story, once the user has overlapped all button tiles.
Use a “text list” array to store strings that will be used to collect user responses.
Use an empty “userResponseList” array to store strings collected from user responses.
Take user input when the Player sprite overlaps a button.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 3 of Orange Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about user input, variables, and arrays. A variable stores one piece of information, while an array stores multiple pieces of information, of the same data type, in an ordered list. Variables and arrays can take in information while they are being created, while the program is running, and from user input. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 3:

badges.title: Save the Data
badges.description: Create variables and arrays to store and use data in a project.

badges.title: Results May Vary
badges.description: Create a new variable and assign it a value.

badges.title: Making a List
badges.description: Create and add items to an array.

badges.title: Dictionary
badges.description: Create and use an array of strings.

badges.title: Art Critic
badges.description: Compare two images to make something happen in a project.
